spatial_claims.claim: D is the centre of circle ABC, lying on diameter AB (inside the circle)
AE is perpendicular to AB at endpoint A, so angle BAE = angle DAE = right angle
CHA is the semicircular arc on the same side of AB as E
Reductio: assume AE enters circle, meeting circumference at C other than A
DA = DC (radii), so triangle DAC is isosceles with angle DAC = angle DCA
Angle DAC is right (AE perpendicular to AB), so angle DCA is also right
FA lies within angle BAE; every point of FA except A is outside the circle
Angle DAF is part of right angle DAE, so angle DAF < right angle
D is inside the circle while FA lies outside except at A, so D is not on FA
DG is perpendicular to FA at G; angle AGD is right
G is not A (otherwise DA perpendicular to FA and angle DAF = right, contradicting Step 6)
In triangle DAG, angle AGD is right so angle DAG < right angle (I.17)
G lies on ray FA (not on FA produced beyond A): if beyond A, angles DAG + DAF = two right angles (I.13), but both < right angle
G is on FA other than A, so G is outside the circle
In triangle AGD: angle AGD (right) > angle DAG, so AD > DG (I.19)
D inside circle and G outside circle, so DG crosses circumference at H between D and G; DG > DH
DH = DA (radii) and DA > DG (Step 9), so DH > DG, contradicting DG > DH
Any line AF within angle BAE meets circumference (otherwise it would be interposed, contradicting Part 2)
Chord AC falls within the circle (3.2), so circumference CHA lies between AF and AE
Angle BAF is part of the angle of the semicircle; remaining angle (circumference to AE) is part of angle FAE
Angle BAF = K < right angle BAE, so AF within angle BAE; angle of semicircle > K
Angle EAF = K < right angle EAB, so AF within angle BAE; remaining angle < K

configuration_map:
Circle ABC with center D and diameter AB. Line AE perpendicular to AB at A extends outside the circle (established Part 1). Semicircular arc CHA lies on the same side of AB as E.

Point D: center of circle, on diameter AB, inside the circle — used consistently throughout as interior point (Steps 1, 7, 10).

Point G (Part 2 reductio): foot of perpendicular from D to line FA. Lies on segment FA (not beyond A — argued in Step 8 by angle sum). Since G is on FA and distinct from A, and FA is outside the circle except at A, G is outside the circle. Used consistently as exterior point (Steps 8, 10).

Point H (Part 2 reductio): intersection of segment DG with circumference. Since D is inside and G is outside, H lies between D and G on segment DG. DH is a radius. Used consistently as circumference point between D and G (Step 10).

Lines AF (Part 3): Any line from A within angle BAE must cross the circumference (by Part 2 impossibility of interposition). The chord from A to the crossing point falls within the circle (3.2). This places the circumference between AF and AE near A, establishing the angle containment relationships used in Steps 13-14.

All point positions (inside/outside/on circle) and angle orderings are maintained consistently across all steps.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The proof carefully tracks point positions relative to the circle (D inside, G outside, H on circumference between D and G) and angle orderings (DAF < right, DAG < right, AGD = right). The Step 8 argument correctly establishes G on ray FA rather than beyond A. Contradictions arising in the reductio arguments (Parts 1 and 2) are intentional consequences of the false assumptions, not proof errors. The Part 3 direct argument using I.23 and 3.2 is a legitimate alternative to Heath's reductio approach, with sound spatial reasoning throughout.
